p1.key: From pV = (m/M)RT, M = mRT/(pV). Use T in kelvin (35 + 273 = 308 K) and V in cm<sup>3</sup> (250) to match R in cm<sup>3</sup> atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>: M = 1.42 × 82.05 × 308 / (250 × 0.85).
Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure. Total = 0.80 mol, so x(O2) = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25 and p(O2) = 0.25 × 1.6 = 0.40 atm. 0.25 is the mole fraction, not the pressure.
p1.flag: partial pressures (Dalton's law) not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Volume fraction equals mole fraction for gases. Partial pressure = 0.01 × 101 kPa = 1.01 kPa.
p1.flag: partial pressures (Dalton's law) not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Gases compress easily because most of the volume is empty space: the molecules themselves take up a tiny fraction of it. The other statements are true but do not explain compressibility.
pV = (m/M)RT, so density m/V = PM<sub>r</sub>/(RT).

M = mRT/(pV), with T = 25 + 273 = 298 K and V = 125 cm<sup>3</sup> to match R in cm<sup>3</sup> atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>: M = 0.725 × 82.05 × 298/(0.97 × 125). C uses V in dm<sup>3</sup>, which does not match R.
Gases are most ideal when intermolecular forces are smallest (non-polar molecules) and the particles have high kinetic energy and are far apart: high temperature and low pressure.
p ∝ T/V. Doubling V and halving T divides p by 4. B and C leave p unchanged, and D only doubles it.
At constant temperature the average speed of the particles is unchanged and the particles themselves don't change size; increasing pressure reduces the volume, so the particles are closer together.

Density = mass/volume. In a sealed rigid container neither mass nor volume changes, so density stays constant. Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy and speed of the molecules, and so the pressure.
M = mRT/pV (from pV = nRT with n = m/M), so pressure, temperature and volume must all be known along with the mass.
Mole fraction of N2 = 0.6/1.2 = 0.5. Partial pressure = 0.5 × 2.0 atm = 1.0 atm.
V = nRT/p: volume is largest when temperature is high and pressure is low.
At constant pressure V ∝ T (in kelvin). Doubling V from 20.0 to 40.0 dm3 needs T to double: 300 K → 600 K = 327 °C. Doubling °C (54 °C) is the trap.
V ∝ T/p. Halving the pressure doubles V and doubling the temperature doubles V again, giving 4 × the volume. In A and B the effects cancel; C reduces V.

p1.key: V = nRT/p: volume is proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to pressure, so high temperature and low pressure give the largest volume.
V2 = V1 × (T2/T1) × (p1/p2) = 2.0 × 2 × ¼ = 1.0 dm3.
V ∝ T/p. Doubling both T and p leaves T/p unchanged, so the volume stays 800 cm3.
p ∝ T/V. Doubling both T and V leaves T/V unchanged, so the pressure stays 40 kPa.
V ∝ T/p (pV = nRT). Doubling both T and p gives V × 2/2, so the volume stays the same.
At constant pressure V ∝ T (in kelvin). V2 = 1 dm³ × (64 + 273)/(32 + 273) = 1 × 337/305 = 1.1 dm³. Option D wrongly uses °C (64/32).
pV/T is constant: (2P × 2V)/T2 = PV/T1, so T2 = 4T1.
pV = (m/M)RT, so M = mRT/pV, with SI units: p = 1.01 × 105 Pa, V = 75 × 10−6 m3, T = 298 K. C. A uses °C and non-SI units; D is inverted.
At constant pressure V ∝ T (in kelvin). Doubling V doubles T: 300 K → 600 K = 327 °C. B (54.0) wrongly doubles the Celsius temperature.

The curve shows inverse proportionality (y ∝ 1/x). For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pV = constant (Boyle's law): pressure on x, volume on y. Temperature and volume (D) or pressure (A) are directly proportional.
At constant pressure V ∝ T (in kelvin): V = 1.0 dm³ × 323 K ÷ 298 K = 1.08 ≈ 1.1 dm³. Doubling to 2.0 wrongly uses °C.
At constant pressure V ∝ T in kelvin. 27.0 °C = 300 K; doubling to 600 K = 327 °C doubles the volume. Doubling the Celsius value (54 °C) does not; doubling pressure halves the volume.
Boyle's law: pV = constant, so V = constant × 1/P (III). A plot of V against P is a curve (I), and V against 1/P is a straight line through the origin (II). All three are correct.
Boyle's law: at constant T, pV = constant, so V ∝ 1/p. A plot of V against 1/p is a straight line through the origin. V against p would be a curve, not a straight line.

Equal amounts of gas need equal pV/T. For the O2: 1.0 × 100 / 300 K. In D: 2.0 × 100 / 600 K gives the same value. Doubling the pressure is cancelled by doubling the Kelvin temperature (27 °C = 300 K, 327 °C = 600 K).
Convert to kelvin: 127 °C = 400 K. At constant pressure V ∝ T, so doubling the volume needs the absolute temperature doubled: 2 × 400 = 800 K. Doubling the Celsius value (254) is a common error.

n = pV/RT and m = nM, so m = MpV/RT. In SI units V = 2.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> cm<sup>3</sup> = 2.00 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup> and T = 298 K: m = 44 × 1.01 × 10<sup>5</sup> × 2.00 × 10<sup>−3</sup>/(8.31 × 298).

At high pressure the gas is compressed, so the volume of the molecules themselves is no longer negligible compared with the container volume, which contradicts an ideal-gas assumption. (Intermolecular attractions also become significant.)
Molar volume (V/n = RT/p) depends only on pressure and temperature. For an ideal gas it is the same whatever the gas is, so its formula does not matter.

With p, V and R constant, nT = pV/R = constant, so n is inversely proportional to T. Plotting n against T gives a hyperbola (D). A straight line through the origin (A) would be direct proportionality.
n(H2) = 10 000 g ÷ 2 g mol−1 = 5 × 103 mol; T = 298 K; V = 1.0 m3. p = nRT/V = 5 × 103 × 8.31 × 298 ÷ 1.0 Pa. Temperature must be in kelvin and mass in grams.

For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pV = constant (Boyle's law), so pressure is inversely proportional to volume: a curve (hyperbola) as in A. B is a straight line with negative slope, which is not inverse proportionality.
At constant pressure V ∝ T (in kelvin). T2 = 300 K × 9.0/10.0 = 270 K = −3.0 °C. Option B (24.3 °C) comes from wrongly using °C directly.
Boyle's law at constant T: p1V1 = p2V2. V2 = 400 × 100 ÷ 200 = 200 cm3; halving the pressure doubles the volume.
At the same temperature both gases have the same average kinetic energy (½mv2). X has a lower average speed, so its particles must have the greater mass, meaning X has the higher molar mass.
p1.flag: Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution for different gases (2025 syllabus uses energy distribution)

p1.key: With p, V and R constant, nT = pV/R is constant, so n is inversely proportional to T: a curve (hyperbola), not a straight line.
For a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant temperature, pV = nRT is constant (Boyle's law), so a graph of pV against p is a horizontal line.
